grammar.title: Tag questions
grammar.explanation_pt:
**Tag questions** são as perguntinhas no fim da frase, como o nosso **"né?"**, **"não é?"**, **"certo?"**. Servem para **confirmar** algo ou **puxar conversa**.

**Regra de ouro:** frase **afirmativa** → tag **negativa**; frase **negativa** → tag **afirmativa**.

A tag repete o **auxiliar** (ou to be / modal) da frase e usa um **pronome**:
- It**'s** cold, **isn't it**?
- You **work** here, **don't you**? (simple present → do/does)
- She **went** home, **didn't she**? (simple past → did)
- They **can** swim, **can't they**?
- You **haven't** been to Japan, **have you**?
- He **won't** come, **will he**?

**Casos especiais:**
- **I am** → **aren't I**? ("I'm late, aren't I?")
- **Let's** → **shall we**? ("Let's go, shall we?")
- Imperativo → **will you?** ("Close the door, will you?")
- **There is** → **isn't there**?

**Entonação:** voz **descendo** ↘ = você tem certeza, só quer concordância (small talk). Voz **subindo** ↗ = pergunta real, você não tem certeza.

examples.en: This coffee is really good, isn't it? ↘
examples.pt: Esse café é muito bom, né?
Você é irmão da Paula, não é? (dúvida real)

examples.en: We haven't met before, have we?
examples.pt: A gente não se conhece, né?

grammar.tip_pt: Na dúvida, falantes nativos usam formas informais como **"..., right?"** ou **"..., yeah?"** — funcionam com qualquer frase e são ótimas para começar.

common_mistakes.wrong: You live in Recife, isn't it?
common_mistakes.right: You live in Recife, don't you?
common_mistakes.why_pt: A tag repete o auxiliar da frase (simple present → do), não é sempre "isn't it".
A tag de I am é a exceção: aren't I.

pronunciation.tip_pt: A mesma frase muda de sentido pela entonação. **"You're coming, aren't you? ↘"** (tenho certeza, confirmando). **"You're coming, aren't you? ↗"** (não tenho certeza, quero saber). No small talk, quase sempre é ↘.
practice: You work in marketing, don't you? ↗

reading.title: Why small talk matters
reading.text: Many people hate small talk. "It's superficial," they say. But research in psychology suggests the opposite: short, friendly conversations with strangers — the barista, a neighbor, someone on the train — can make us happier and less lonely. In one study, commuters who talked to a stranger reported a more positive journey than those who sat in silence, even though most of them expected the opposite. Small talk is also the first step to deeper conversations: we rarely make friends or business contacts without it. The secret is curiosity. Ask open questions ("What brings you here?"), listen to the answer, and ask a follow-up. Safe topics include the weather, the place you're in, travel, food and work. Avoid politics, religion, money and personal appearance — at least until you know the person better.

questions.answer: Politics, religion, money, personal appearance.

writing.task: Write a short guide (100–120 words) for a foreign colleague: "How to make small talk in Brazil" — safe topics, topics to avoid and three useful phrases.

writing.model: Small talk in Brazil is easy — Brazilians love to chat! Good topics are food, football, music, travel and the weather (especially if it's very hot). People will probably ask where you're from and if you like Brazil — say yes! Brazilians are usually comfortable with personal questions about family, but avoid politics with people you've just met: it can get heated. Three useful phrases: "Tudo bem?" (How are you?), "Que calor, né?" (It's so hot, isn't it?) and "Você é de onde?" (Where are you from?). Finally, don't be surprised if people stand close or touch your arm when they talk — it's just friendliness.

culture_note.title: "Have a good one!"
culture_note.text_pt: Para encerrar conversas curtas nos EUA, são comuns **"Have a good one!"**, **"Take care!"** e **"Catch you later!"**. No Reino Unido, ouve-se **"Cheers!"** (obrigado/tchau) e **"Mind how you go!"**. E o famoso **"Nice weather, isn't it?"** é quase um esporte nacional britânico.

grammar.title: Present perfect: experiências
grammar.explanation_pt:
O **present perfect** liga o passado ao presente. O primeiro uso: **experiências de vida**, quando **não importa quando** aconteceu — só se aconteceu ou não.

**Estrutura:** **have / has** + **particípio passado**
- I**'ve** (I have) **been** to Chile.
- She**'s** (she has) **eaten** snails.
- I **haven't** seen that movie. / He **hasn't** flown before.
- **Have** you **ever** **tried** surfing?

**Particípio:** regulares = igual ao passado (-ed): worked, visited, tried. Irregulares têm uma **terceira forma** (go – went – **gone**, see – saw – **seen**, eat – ate – **eaten**). Revise a lista de verbos!

**Ever** (alguma vez) aparece em perguntas: Have you **ever**...? **Never** (nunca) em afirmativas com sentido negativo: I've **never**...

**Been x gone:**
- She's **been** to Paris. (foi e já voltou — experiência)
- She's **gone** to Paris. (foi e ainda está lá)

**Present perfect → simple past:** a pergunta de experiência usa present perfect, mas quando você dá **detalhes** (quando, onde, como foi), muda para o **simple past**:
"Have you ever been to Peru?" "Yes, I **have**. I **went** in 2022. It **was** amazing."

rows: Have you ever been to Japan?
Yes, I have. / No, I haven't.
Has she ever met a celebrity?
Yes, she has. / No, she hasn't.

examples.en: Have you ever ridden a camel? — Yes, once, in Morocco. It was hilarious!
examples.pt: Você já andou de camelo? — Sim, uma vez, no Marrocos. Foi hilário!

examples.en: I've never lived abroad, but I've traveled a lot.
examples.pt: Nunca morei fora, mas já viajei muito.

examples.en: My parents have been to Portugal three times.
examples.pt: Meus pais já foram a Portugal três vezes.

grammar.tip_pt: **Nunca** use present perfect com tempo passado definido (yesterday, in 2019, last year, when I was a child). Nesses casos, é simple past: "I **went** to Rio **in 2019**" (e não "I've been to Rio in 2019").

common_mistakes.wrong: Did you ever go to London?
common_mistakes.right: Have you ever been to London?
common_mistakes.why_pt: Para experiências de vida, sem tempo definido, use present perfect.

common_mistakes.wrong: I've been to Bahia last year.
common_mistakes.right: I went to Bahia last year.
common_mistakes.why_pt: Com tempo definido (last year), use simple past.
Present perfect usa o particípio (eaten), não o passado (ate).

pronunciation.tip_pt: Na fala, **have** quase sempre vira **'ve** ("áiv", "uív", "dêiv") e **has** vira **'s**. O **'ve** é bem curto — às vezes só um "v" leve: "I've been" = "áivbin". **Been** é fraco: "bin" (EUA), não "bíin".

reading.title: Experiences vs. things
reading.text: Have you ever wondered why a trip makes you happier than a new phone? Psychologists who study happiness have found that spending money on experiences — travel, concerts, courses, dinners with friends — usually brings more lasting happiness than spending on things. One reason is adaptation: we get used to new objects quickly, but memories of experiences often get better with time. Another reason is connection: experiences are usually shared with other people and become part of our identity and our stories. "I've climbed a volcano" says more about who you are than "I've bought a new TV." Of course, things matter too — but next time you have some extra money, consider buying a memory instead of an object.

grammar.title: Be supposed to · It's + adjetivo + to + verbo
grammar.explanation_pt:
**Be supposed to + verbo** = o que é **esperado** por regra, costume ou combinação ("é para...", "deveria"):
- In Japan, you**'re supposed to** bow when you greet someone.
- You**'re not supposed to** eat on the subway in Singapore.
- **Am I supposed to** tip here?
- No passado = o que deveria ter acontecido (e não aconteceu): "I **was supposed to** call her, but I forgot."

**It's + adjetivo + to + verbo** para falar de costumes:
- **It's polite to** bring flowers.
- **It's rude to** blow your nose at the table.
- **It's customary to** shake hands.
- **It's (not) acceptable to** arrive late.
- **It's common to** kiss on the cheek.

Para negar o costume, use **not**: "It's **not** polite **to**..." ou "You'**re not supposed to**...". Para opções: "You **don't have to** tip, but you **can**."

rows: You're supposed to arrive on time.
You're not supposed to touch the art.
The train was supposed to leave at 8.
It's polite to say thank you.

dialogue.title: Dinner in Tokyo
dialogue.context_pt: Caio vai jantar na casa de um colega japonês e pede dicas a uma amiga que morou no Japão.

lines.speaker: Caio
lines.en: Yuki, I'm going to have dinner at my coworker's house in Tokyo. What am I supposed to do?
lines.pt: Yuki, vou jantar na casa de um colega em Tóquio. O que eu devo fazer?

lines.speaker: Yuki
lines.en: First, you're supposed to take off your shoes at the entrance. They'll give you slippers.
lines.pt: Primeiro, você deve tirar os sapatos na entrada. Eles vão te dar chinelos.

lines.speaker: Caio
lines.en: OK. Should I bring a gift?
lines.pt: OK. Devo levar um presente?

lines.speaker: Yuki
lines.en: Yes, it's customary to bring something small, like sweets. And it's polite to offer it with both hands.
lines.pt: Sim, é costume levar algo pequeno, como doces. E é educado oferecer com as duas mãos.

lines.speaker: Caio
lines.en: Good to know. What about chopsticks? I'm terrible with them.
lines.pt: Bom saber. E os hashis? Sou péssimo com eles.

lines.speaker: Yuki
lines.en: Just don't stick them upright in your rice. It's associated with funerals, so it's considered very rude.
lines.pt: Só não espete eles em pé no arroz. É associado a funerais, então é considerado muito grosseiro.

lines.speaker: Caio
lines.en: Wow. And am I supposed to finish everything on my plate?
lines.pt: Uau. E devo comer tudo do prato?

lines.speaker: Consultant
lines.en: Let's look at three countries. In Germany, you're supposed to be exactly on time — five minutes late is considered rude. People usually use last names and titles, like Herr Doktor Schmidt, until invited to use first names. In the United States, it's common to use first names right away, and small talk before a meeting is short. In China, it's polite to receive a business card with both hands and look at it carefully. You're not supposed to write on it or put it in your back pocket. Remember: when in doubt, observe and copy your hosts.

reading.title: Tipping around the world
reading.text: Tipping is one of the most confusing parts of traveling. In the United States, servers depend on tips because their salaries are low, so you're supposed to leave 15 to 20 percent in restaurants. Not tipping is seen as very rude. In Japan, it's the opposite: tipping can be considered strange or even insulting, because good service is simply expected. In most of Europe, a service charge is often included in the bill, and leaving a few extra coins is a nice gesture but not required. In Brazil, restaurants usually add 10% to the bill, and you can choose not to pay it — although most people do. The golden rule? Check the local custom before you travel, and when you're not sure, ask: "Is service included?"

questions.q: Why are you supposed to tip in the US?
questions.answer: Because servers depend on tips (their salaries are low).

questions.q: How can tipping be seen in Japan?
questions.answer: As strange or even insulting.

questions.q: What's the situation in most of Europe?
questions.answer: A service charge is often included; extra coins are nice but not required.

questions.q: What question can you ask when you're not sure?
questions.answer: "Is service included?"

grammar.title: Do you mind if...? / Would you mind if...?
grammar.explanation_pt:
Para pedir **permissão** de forma educada:
- **Do you mind if** I + **simple present**? → "Do you mind if I **call** you Ana?"
- **Would you mind if** I + **simple past**? (mais formal) → "Would you mind if I **called** you Ana?"

⚠️ **Atenção à resposta!** "Mind" significa "se importar". Então:
- **"No, not at all." / "No, go ahead."** = **pode sim** (não me importo) ✅
- **"Yes, I do mind." / "Actually, I'd rather you didn't."** = **não pode** ❌

Para pedir que **outra pessoa** faça algo: **Would you mind + verbo-ing?** → "Would you mind **spelling** your name?"

**Títulos:**
- **Mr.** (homens) + sobrenome: Mr. Smith
- **Ms.** (mulheres — neutro, o mais seguro no trabalho) + sobrenome: Ms. Lopez
- **Mrs.** (mulher casada) / **Miss** (jovem/solteira — pouco usado hoje)
- **Dr.** + sobrenome (médicos e doutores) · **Professor** + sobrenome (professores universitários)
- Nunca use título + primeiro nome: ❌ "Mr. John" (comum no Brasil, estranho em inglês) → ✅ "Mr. Smith" ou "John".

No, not at all. / Go ahead.

listening.title: Email etiquette tips
listening.context_pt: Um professor de inglês para negócios explica como começar e terminar e-mails.

lines.speaker: Teacher
lines.en: The way you open and close an email shows your tone. For a formal email to someone you don't know, start with "Dear Mr. Lee" or "Dear Ms. Santos". If you don't know the name, "Dear Hiring Manager" is better than "To whom it may concern", which sounds old-fashioned. For colleagues, "Hi Ana" is perfect. Close formal emails with "Kind regards" or "Best regards". "Cheers" is friendly, especially in the UK and Australia, but don't use it with a new client. And please — never write "Kisses" or "Hugs" in a business email, even if Brazilians do it with friends!

questions.answer: "Dear Mr. Lee" / "Dear Ms. Santos".

questions.answer: "Dear Hiring Manager".

questions.q: When is "Cheers" OK?
questions.answer: With colleagues/friendly contacts (especially in the UK and Australia), not new clients.

questions.q: What should you never write in a business email?

reading.title: Is "Mr." disappearing?
reading.text: In many English-speaking workplaces, titles are becoming less common. Tech companies in Silicon Valley are famous for their informal culture: the CEO is "Mark" or "Sundar", and nobody wears a tie. Many universities and hospitals, however, still prefer titles like "Professor" and "Dr.", especially with students and patients. In the UK, older generations often expect "Mr." or "Mrs." until they say otherwise. Another change is the use of "Ms." instead of "Mrs." or "Miss": it doesn't reveal whether a woman is married, and it's now the standard in professional situations. Some people prefer gender-neutral titles like "Mx." The safest strategy? Follow the other person's lead. If someone signs an email "Jennifer", you can reply "Hi Jennifer". If they sign "Dr. Jennifer Adams", start with "Dear Dr. Adams".

questions.q: Where are titles becoming less common?
questions.answer: In many English-speaking workplaces, especially tech companies.

questions.q: Where are titles still preferred?
questions.answer: In universities and hospitals (with students and patients) and with older generations in the UK.

questions.q: Why is "Ms." the standard now?
questions.answer: It doesn't reveal whether a woman is married.

questions.q: What's the safest strategy?
questions.answer: Follow the other person's lead (how they sign their emails).
